promptText: What primary problem does Spring AI's PromptTemplate solve compared to plain string concatenation for building prompts?
options: It separates the fixed shape of a prompt from its variable data, enabling reuse, testing, and externalization
It automatically improves the accuracy of the model's response
It compresses the prompt to reduce token count
It encrypts the prompt text before sending it to the model
explanation: PromptTemplate is a text-assembly abstraction, not an AI-specific invention: it lets you name placeholders, externalize wording, and unit test rendering, none of which raw concatenation gives you for free.

promptText: By default, what templating engine powers Spring AI's PromptTemplate rendering, and what placeholder syntax does it use?
options: Handlebars, using double curly braces {{name}}
StringTemplate (ST), using single curly braces {name}
Freemarker, using ${name}
A custom Spring AI regex engine, using %name%
explanation: Spring AI wraps the mature StringTemplate (ST) engine, created by Terence Parr, using its single-curly-brace placeholder syntax rather than inventing a new templating language.

promptText: What is the key difference between PromptTemplate.render() and PromptTemplate.create()?
options: render() calls the model directly; create() only builds text
render() returns a plain substituted String; create() wraps the rendered text into a full Prompt object
They are functionally identical; create() is just deprecated
create() validates the JSON schema of the model output; render() does not
explanation: render() performs only text substitution and returns a String, while create() goes further and wraps that rendered text into a Prompt (typically as a UserMessage) ready for a ChatModel.

promptText: Why would a team back a PromptTemplate with an externalized classpath Resource file instead of an inline Java string literal?
options: Inline strings can't include placeholders at all
Resource files execute faster because they skip the StringTemplate parser
It decouples prompt wording from compiled code, letting it be reviewed and edited (even by non-engineers) without a redeploy
Only Resource-backed templates can be reused across multiple ChatClient calls
explanation: Externalizing to a Resource file lets prompt wording be reviewed as its own diff and edited by non-Java-fluent prompt specialists without touching compiled code or requiring a rebuild.

promptText: If a PromptTemplate references {customerName} but the Map<String,Object> passed to render() has no such key, what happens?
options: The placeholder silently renders as an empty string
The literal text "{customerName}" is left in the output
Rendering fails fast with an exception
Spring AI substitutes a default value of "null"
explanation: Missing keys cause rendering to fail fast rather than silently producing a blank or malformed slot, because a loud immediate failure is far easier to catch than a quietly broken prompt.

promptText: A placeholder is filled with an Integer instead of a String. What actually gets substituted into the rendered text?
options: Rendering throws a type-mismatch exception immediately
The value's toString() representation
The value is automatically JSON-encoded
Spring AI silently drops non-String values from the map
explanation: The renderer substitutes each value's toString() form regardless of its original type, which is harmless for numbers but can produce awkward output for objects like Lists with a default toString().

promptText: A template string contains the literal instruction: Return JSON like {"category": ...}. Why does this commonly break during rendering?
options: StringTemplate doesn't support JSON output at all
The default renderer treats curly braces as placeholder delimiters, so the literal JSON braces are misread as variable slots
JSON strings must be Base64-encoded before templating
PromptTemplate strips all punctuation from the rendered text
explanation: Because the default StringTemplate-based renderer uses curly braces as its delimiter, literal JSON braces collide with placeholder syntax and must be escaped or handled with an alternative TemplateRenderer.

promptText: In PromptTemplate documentation and source, a render() method takes a parameter conventionally called 'model' (a Map<String,Object>). What does 'model' mean in this context?
options: The foundation LLM (e.g., which ChatModel to call)
The MVC-style data map of substitution values, unrelated to the foundation model
A serialized copy of the ChatOptions
The embedding model used for the prompt
explanation: In templating vocabulary inherited from MVC, 'model' means the map of key-value substitution data, not the foundation model, a deliberate but easy-to-confuse overload of the word.

promptText: Why should a Spring Boot service cache constructed PromptTemplate instances (e.g., as singleton beans) rather than building a fresh one from a raw string on every request?
options: PromptTemplate objects hold an open network connection to the model provider
Constructing and parsing a template on every request wastes CPU cycles unnecessarily since parsing is decoupled from per-request rendering
Spring AI enforces a hard limit on how many PromptTemplate instances can exist
Uncached templates cannot use externalized Resource files
explanation: Parsing a template is not free; treating the parsed PromptTemplate as an expensive-ish, cacheable singleton and rendering as the cheap per-request step is the correct production pattern.

promptText: Why is placing untrusted, user-supplied content into a UserMessage-backed template generally safer than interpolating the same content into a SystemMessage-backed template?
options: UserMessage content is automatically sanitized by Spring AI before rendering
SystemMessage templates don't support placeholders
The model is primed to treat system-role text as more authoritative instruction, so mixing untrusted data there raises prompt-injection risk more than in a clearly-delimited user-role slot
UserMessage templates have a smaller token budget, limiting injected attack payloads
explanation: Templating substitutes text with no notion of trust, so role placement is the practical mitigation: content framed as 'data to analyze' in a UserMessage is safer than the same content inside an authoritative SystemMessage.

promptText: A team's JSON-heavy prompts keep colliding with StringTemplate's curly-brace delimiters. Besides manually escaping every literal brace, what's the other supported fix?
options: Disable the templating engine and hand-write string concatenation instead
Configure a different TemplateRenderer (e.g., a Mustache-style double-brace renderer) whose delimiter doesn't collide with JSON syntax
Wrap all JSON output in XML instead
Switch the model provider to one that doesn't emit JSON
explanation: Spring AI's rendering is pluggable behind a TemplateRenderer interface, so configuring an alternative renderer with a non-colliding delimiter scheme avoids fighting the default engine's escaping rules entirely.

promptText: A value substituted into a template happens to itself contain curly braces (e.g., a JSON blob returned from a tool call). What happens to those braces in the rendered output?
options: They are re-parsed as further template placeholders, potentially causing a second substitution pass
They pass through untouched as plain text, since substitution happens once into already-parsed template structure
Rendering throws an exception because nested braces are never allowed in substituted values
They are automatically escaped with a backslash by the renderer
explanation: Substitution happens once into an already-parsed template; braces arriving as part of a substituted value's content are not treated as new template syntax.

promptText: Two independently-authored fragment templates both use the placeholder {name} for different things. Under what condition does this actually cause a bug when composed into an outer template?
options: It's always a bug, because {name} is a globally reserved StringTemplate identifier
It's only a bug if both fragments are merged into one template source and rendered together against a single shared map -- if each fragment is rendered independently first, there's no collision
It's never a bug because Spring AI automatically namespaces placeholders per fragment
It's only a bug when the values are non-String objects
explanation: If each fragment is rendered independently against its own map before the results are concatenated as plain strings, there is no collision; the risk only appears when both fragments share one render pass against one map.

promptText: A colleague argues that since PromptTemplate rendering is deterministic, unit testing it is unnecessary -- the real risk is the model's response. What's the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Rendering is not actually deterministic across JVM restarts

Rendering failures and defects (missing escapes, wrong variable, malformed data) are an entirely separate, avoidable source of variance from the model's inherent non-determinism, and conflating the two makes it impossible to tell which is responsible when output quality drifts
Unit tests for rendering require a live model call anyway, so there's no cost savings
PromptTemplate does not expose a way to inspect rendered output in tests
explanation: PromptTemplate's job is to make prompt assembly boringly reliable so that when quality changes, you can trust it is a model or content problem, not a plumbing problem -- something only testable if assembly is actually tested.

promptText: Why does designing a template so its stable instructional content appears first and variable, data-dependent content appears last provide a real production benefit beyond code cleanliness?
options: StringTemplate parses templates faster when placeholders occur later in the string
It aligns with prompt-caching mechanisms some model providers offer for requests whose prefix is byte-identical to a recent previous request, reducing cost/latency for the stable portion
It guarantees the model reads the system instructions before the user's question
It reduces the chance of curly-brace collisions with JSON content
explanation: A template that renders the same fixed prefix every time and varies only the trailing content is naturally friendlier to provider-side prompt-caching discounts than ad hoc concatenation that might reorder content unpredictably.
